pages.title: INTRODUCTION
pages.html:
INTRODUCTION

The Long Game

BDM work is not about the meeting. It is about everything that makes the meeting worth having.

The Business Development Manager is the most misunderstood professional in any organization.

They are not sales. Not quite. They are not marketing. Not entirely. They are not account management, though they manage accounts. They are not strategy, though their work shapes it. What the BDM actually is — what the BDM does that no one else can fully replace — is build the conditions under which revenue becomes possible before anyone knows it is coming.

The BDM's conversations do not produce invoices. They produce pipelines. They produce referrals that arrive six months after the lunch that created them. They produce partnerships that generate three years of revenue from a relationship that started as a cold introduction. They produce the deal that closes because of a trust account that was built so carefully, over so many small scored conversations, that when the moment came the other person did not even consider calling anyone else.

That is BDM work. And every single piece of it lives in conversation.

◆

Profit. Love. Tax.

The BDM's scoring environment is different from every other Scorer edition in one fundamental way: the time horizon. In real estate, the score resolves at closing — usually within thirty to sixty days. In politics, the score resolves at the vote. In BDM work, a single conversation may not produce a visible score movement for six months. The BDM who measures their conversations by what happened in the room is measuring the wrong thing.

The BDM measures by what the conversation made possible. Not today. Eventually.

This book teaches you to score those long-game conversations in real time — to see the Profit building, the Love accumulating, the Tax that is quietly compounding in relationships you thought were strong. It gives you the nine moves. It gives you the full cast of characters in the BDM world. And it gives you a field guide for every situation in the business development lifecycle — from the cold introduction to the referral that changes your year.

The BDM who reads this book stops managing relationships and starts scoring them. Those are not the same job.

pages.title: PART ONE
pages.html:
PART ONE

The BDM World

What business development actually is. What it is not. What makes it the most relationship-dependent profession alive.

pages.title: CHAPTER 1
pages.html:
CHAPTER 1

The Pipeline Nobody Sees

Every deal in your pipeline started with a conversation that did not look like a deal.

It looked like a lunch. A conference introduction. A follow-up email that took three drafts. A phone call where the other person said "let's stay in touch" and you said "absolutely" and you both meant something slightly different by both words. That conversation — unremarkable at the time, invisible on any activity report — was the beginning of the score that eventually produced the revenue.

The BDM who cannot see that conversation clearly cannot develop the conversation that follows it correctly. They call too soon. Or too late. They ask for the meeting before the Love account justifies asking. They pitch before they have built the Profit position that makes the pitch credible. They lose relationships they did not know they were losing because they were tracking activity instead of scores.

◆

The BDM pipeline is not a funnel. It is a ledger.

Every interaction with every contact either deposits into or withdraws from three accounts simultaneously — Profit, Love, and Tax. A lunch that provides genuine value deposits Love. A follow-up that asks for something before it gives something withdraws Profit. A promise about timeline that does not get met deposits Tax. None of these movements are visible in a CRM entry. All of them determine whether the relationship produces revenue or quietly goes cold.

The scorer sees the ledger. The scorer knows the balance in every relationship before they pick up the phone.

pages.title: CHAPTER 2
pages.html:
CHAPTER 2

Why BDM Pipelines Go Cold

A pipeline does not go cold because the market changed. It goes cold because scores drained and nobody noticed.

The Profit collapsed. The BDM lost their expert position. They stopped bringing relevant intelligence to their contacts and started arriving with their own agenda visible. The contact began to sense that conversations with this BDM were designed to produce an outcome for the BDM rather than create value for them. Once a contact understands — consciously or not — that you need something from them more than you are giving something to them, Profit inverts. You are no longer in the room as a peer. You are in the room as someone who wants something. Pipelines built on inverted Profit do not close. They stall.

The Love burned. Slowly. In the accumulation of small moments where the BDM was present without being genuinely useful. The check-in call with nothing new to say. The "just touching base" email that touches no base worth touching. The quarterly lunch that both parties attend out of obligation rather than genuine value. Love does not burn in BDM relationships with a dramatic moment. It burns in the growing recognition that the relationship has become transactional rather than generative.

The Tax became invisible and then unbearable. The contact who has been referred several times but never reciprocated starts to feel the imbalance even if they never name it. The BDM who consistently asks for introductions without providing them has built a Tax position they do not see on their own balance sheet — but the contact absolutely sees it on theirs. When the Tax becomes high enough, the contact finds reasons to be unavailable that they cannot fully articulate. They are not being dishonest. They are exiting a relationship whose cost has exceeded its value.

◆

The scorer sees all three before they become invisible on the activity report. Because every cold pipeline tells the same story: scores drained in the conversations that appeared to be going fine.

pages.title: PART TWO
pages.html:
PART TWO

The Six Characters

The complete BDM relationship ecosystem. Everyone whose score matters.

01

The Partner

The Partner is the BDM's most important relationship and most commonly misread one.

A Partner is not a client. They are not a vendor. They are a peer professional whose work intersects with yours often enough that mutual referral is natural, whose clients are adjacent to your clients, and whose reputation either amplifies or diminishes your own depending on the quality of the association. The right Partner multiplies your pipeline. The wrong Partner attaches their problems to your reputation.

The Partner relationship runs on symmetry. Both parties must feel that the exchange is roughly balanced — that they are receiving value approximately equal to what they are providing. The moment a Partner relationship becomes asymmetrical, it begins to drain. The BDM who receives more referrals than they send is running a high-Tax position they often cannot see from their own side. The BDM who sends more referrals than they receive is running a Love surplus that is building — but if it builds without reciprocation long enough, it converts to resentment.

◆

Reading the Partner's score: Profit — do they call you when they have information to share, or only when they have something to ask? Partners who share information freely have a high Profit account with you — they see the relationship as generative. Partners who only call when they need something have inverted Profit. Love — how quickly do they return your calls? Response time in a Partner relationship is one of the most accurate Love signals available. Tax — are they comfortable introducing you to their best clients, or do they introduce you to the ones they are less invested in?

02

The Referral Source

The Referral Source is the highest-value relationship in the BDM ecosystem and the one that requires the most precise scoring.

They are not a Partner in the full sense — they may not be in a business that creates natural reciprocal referral. They refer to you because they trust you with their clients. Their clients are their most valuable asset. When a Referral Source sends a client to you, they are lending you their reputation. They are telling their client: this person is as good as I am. They are staking their own Love account on your performance.

The obligation created by a referral is the highest Tax in BDM work. The Referral Source who sends you a client has created an obligation that does not end when the deal closes. It extends to how you treated that client, how you communicated throughout, and whether the client came back to the Referral Source and said "thank you for introducing me to them" or said nothing — which is its own signal.

◆

The BDM who manages Referral Source relationships correctly treats every referred client as a performance in front of the person who sent them. Because it is. The referral did not come from nowhere. It came from a Love account that was built carefully over time and is now being expressed as trust. Honor it accordingly.

Reading the Referral Source's score: Profit — how detailed is their introduction when they refer? A detailed introduction ("I want you to know exactly what Marcus is trying to accomplish and here is why I think you are the right person") signals a high Profit position. A brief introduction signals a relationship that is functioning but not deep. Love — do they follow up after the referral to ask how it went? Tax — do you know anything meaningful about their business beyond what you need to generate referrals?

03

The Prospect

The Prospect is the person who does not know they need you yet.

Not every Prospect has an immediate problem you can solve. Many of them have a problem they are not fully aware of, or a problem they have learned to tolerate, or a future need that has not yet become urgent. The BDM who can only work with Prospects who have an identified, active need is working with a fraction of the actual pipeline available to them. The BDM who can build relationships with Prospects before the need exists — who is present and trusted when the need arrives — is working with the full pipeline.

The Prospect relationship is the purest expression of the long-game BDM philosophy. There is no invoice at the end of a Prospect conversation. There is no commission. There is often no immediate visible output at all. What there is — if the conversation was scored correctly — is a slight increase in the Love account, a small improvement in the Profit position, and a managed Tax that ensures the next conversation is easier than this one.

◆

The single most common BDM error with Prospects: pitching too soon. The BDM who arrives at a first Prospect conversation with a pitch has misread the stage of the relationship. The Prospect has not yet built the Love account that makes a pitch credible. They have not yet experienced enough Intelligence Transfer to know that the BDM has something worth buying. The pitch lands as pressure rather than value. The Prospect politely says they will be in touch. They are not in touch.

Score the Prospect conversation correctly: the goal is Love accumulation and Profit establishment. The pitch is not available until both of those accounts are high enough to make it land.

04

The Agent

The Agent is the BDM's internal client.

In real estate specifically, the BDM exists to build the conditions that make the Agent's pipeline possible. The BDM finds the builder relationships, the relocation accounts, the referral networks that the Agent does not have time to cultivate. The Agent closes the deals. The BDM creates the landscape in which more deals exist to close.

The BDM and Agent relationship runs on one fundamental agreement: the BDM owns the relationship-building and the Agent owns the conversion. When both parties respect that division, the partnership compounds. When either party tries to do the other's job, it creates friction that eventually resolves in one of two ways — renegotiation of roles or dissolution of the partnership.

◆

Reading the Agent's score: Profit — does the Agent take the BDM's pipeline seriously, or do they treat referrals as secondary to their own sourced business? An Agent who does not prioritize BDM referrals appropriately is burning the Referral Source's Love account on the BDM's behalf. Love — does the Agent communicate outcomes back to the BDM so the BDM can report back to the Referral Source? The Agent who closes a deal without telling the BDM how the client was treated has broken the feedback loop that the entire BDM operation runs on. Tax — does the Agent make promises in client conversations that the BDM then has to manage?

05

The Builder / Corporate Partner

The Builder or Corporate Partner is the institutional relationship.

Where individual Partner and Referral Source relationships run on personal trust, the institutional relationship runs on demonstrated value at scale. The builder who sends the BDM their buyers does not do so because they like the BDM personally — though personal trust helps. They do so because the BDM and their team have consistently delivered for builder clients at a level that justifies the continued association.

Institutional relationships are slower to build and slower to lose than personal ones. The Love account accumulates over multiple transactions, multiple agents, multiple clients — and it drains the same way. One bad transaction does not end an institutional relationship. A pattern of bad transactions does. The BDM managing an institutional relationship is managing a portfolio of scores across every interaction between their organization and the institution.

◆

The highest-Profit move in an institutional relationship: proactive communication about problems before they become problems. The builder whose BDM calls them to say "I want to flag something on the Harrison file before it becomes an issue" is receiving something most of their vendor relationships do not provide. That call builds more institutional Love than a year of smooth transactions because it demonstrates a level of engagement that most institutional partners have stopped expecting.

06

The Competitor

The Competitor is the most misused character in the BDM ecosystem.

Most BDMs treat competitors as threats to be defeated or ignored. The scorer treats competitors as information sources and, occasionally, as future partners. In any market of sufficient complexity, the best BDMs know each other. They know who runs a clean operation and who does not. Who sends clients that are prepared and who sends clients that are problems. Whose word means something in a room and whose word requires verification.

pages.title: PART TWO (cont. 2)
pages.html:
The BDM who treats every competitor as an enemy has a smaller map of their market than the one who treats them as professionals operating in the same space. There are competitor conversations worth having — where market intelligence is exchanged, where referral overflow happens, where the relationship produces goodwill that generates business in ways neither party fully anticipated.

◆

Reading the Competitor's score: the BDM who understands that Profit in a competitor conversation comes from information and positioning — not from trying to convert a competitor into a client or partner prematurely — runs these conversations at a level most professionals in their market never develop. The competitor who respects you refers to you. The competitor who trusts you sends you their overflow. The competitor who believes you would handle their clients with the same care they would becomes, in time, something other than a competitor.

pages.title: PART THREE
pages.html:
PART THREE

The Long Game

The BDM's scoring philosophy. Why the timeline changes everything.

The BDM Score Runs on Months

Every other Scorer edition in this series operates on a short score cycle. Real estate transactions resolve in thirty to sixty days. Political campaigns resolve at the vote. Sales conversations resolve in days or weeks. The score in those environments is fast and visible.

The BDM score runs on months. Sometimes years. A single Referral Source relationship, if scored correctly from the first introduction, may not produce visible revenue for six to eighteen months. The Love account that eventually produces that revenue was built in conversations that appeared to produce nothing — the lunch where the BDM asked good questions and said little about themselves, the follow-up that provided value with no ask attached, the call to share information that had no immediate agenda.

The BDM who cannot sit in the discomfort of a long-building score does not last in the role. Not because they lack skill. Because they measure the wrong things. They measure activity when they should be measuring account balances.

◆

Three questions a BDM should ask about every relationship in their portfolio, quarterly:

Has the Profit account moved? Have they seen me demonstrate expertise, bring relevant intelligence, or create value that they could not have created without this relationship? If not, the Profit account has been stagnant — which means it has been draining, because stagnant relationships do not hold steady. They drift.

Has the Love account moved? Has anything happened in this relationship that gave the contact a reason to trust me more than they did last quarter? A difficult conversation handled honestly. A promise made and kept. A moment where I told them something that cost me something to tell them. If not, Love has been coasting — which is the beginning of the slow burn.

What is the Tax position? What has this relationship cost the contact recently? Have I asked for more than I have given? Have I made promises I have not fully kept? Have I been present only when I needed something? If yes to any of these, Tax has been building — and in BDM relationships, Tax that builds invisibly is the most dangerous kind.

The BDM's Signature Move

Of the nine moves in the Scorer doctrine, the BDM runs one more than all others.

Move 03 — the Intelligence Transfer.

The BDM who shows up with information — relevant, specific, timely intelligence that the contact can use — is running the BDM's highest-value move in every conversation. Not pitching. Not asking. Giving. Giving information that improves the contact's position before they knew to ask for it.

The builder contact who gets a call from the BDM saying "I want to flag the new school rezoning before it goes public — it affects two of your communities" is receiving Move 03 in its purest form. They did not ask for this information. They did not know to ask. And the BDM has just built more Love in one phone call than three months of check-in lunches would have produced.

◆

The Intelligence Transfer is the BDM's signature move because it accomplishes three things simultaneously: it builds Profit (the BDM has demonstrated they know things worth knowing), it builds Love (they shared it freely), and it reduces Tax (the contact now owes the BDM less than they would have if they had discovered the information themselves and felt the BDM had withheld it).

The BDM who runs Intelligence Transfer consistently, across every relationship in their portfolio, becomes the person nobody in their network can afford to lose contact with. Not because of what the BDM can sell them. Because of what the BDM tells them.

pages.title: PART FOUR
pages.html:
PART FOUR

The Conversations

The BDM world scored in full. Every relationship. Every stage.

BDM / PARTNER

The Relationship Call

Where partnerships are built or where they quietly start to end

Rachel is a BDM in residential real estate. Marcus is a financial advisor. They have had lunch twice. Marcus has referred one client. Rachel is following up.

◆

Rachel: "I wanted to update you on the Torres family. They closed last week. Clean transaction, and they told me specifically to thank whoever introduced them to us."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 ▲ 6|LOVE 74 ▲ 10|TAX 18 ▼ 4

MOVE REFERRAL CLOSE-OUT — LOVE BUILD

Rachel ran the most important post-referral move in BDM work: she closed the loop. She told the Referral Source what happened to their client. Love builds 10 points because Marcus just learned that Rachel treats his clients the way he would want them treated — and that she reports back. Tax drops because the obligation created by the referral has been honored.

Marcus: "Good to hear. They were nervous about the timeline."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 —|LOVE 76 ▲ 2|TAX 16 ▼ 2

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — CONTACT IS INVESTED

Marcus disclosed something about the client's emotional state. This is a Love signal — he trusts Rachel enough to share that the client was anxious, which means he trusts that Rachel handled it. The scorer notes: Marcus is evaluating whether Rachel can be trusted with his more complex clients.

Rachel: "They were. I want to tell you something I noticed working with them — they are going to need estate planning in the next two years based on what they are building. I don't know if that falls in your wheelhouse or if you have someone you'd refer them to, but I wanted to flag it for you before they figure that out on their own."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 82 ▲ 10|LOVE 88 ▲ 12|TAX 12 ▼ 4

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER — MOVE 03 AT FULL EXPRESSION

Rachel just ran the BDM's signature move. She identified a future need in Marcus's client and brought it to him before he knew to look for it. Profit builds because she has demonstrated that she sees beyond the transaction. Love builds 12 points — one of the largest single movements in this book — because she gave Marcus something of genuine value with no visible agenda attached. Tax drops because the relationship has just become generative rather than transactional.

Marcus: "Actually — estate planning is exactly what I do. Can I reach back out to them?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 86 ▲ 4|LOVE 90 ▲ 2|TAX 10 ▼ 2

MOVE RECIPROCAL ENGAGEMENT — PARTNERSHIP FORMS

The partnership just became real. Marcus is now running business development through Rachel the same way she is running it through him. The reciprocal referral loop is open. The scorer marks this as the highest-value outcome of a BDM partner conversation: mutual pipeline creation from a single intelligent move.

BDM / PROSPECT

The First Meeting

Where the pitch is almost always the wrong move

Devon is a BDM. Alicia is the corporate relocation coordinator for a mid-sized tech company. They were introduced at a conference. This is their first one-on-one meeting.

◆

Devon: "Before I tell you anything about what we do — I want to understand what your biggest challenge is right now with relocations. Not what the ideal would look like. The actual current problem."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 8|LOVE 68 ▲ 6|TAX 14 ▼ 4

MOVE DIAGNOSTIC OPENING — PROFIT AND LOVE BUILD

Devon ran the correct opening for a first Prospect meeting: he asked a diagnostic question instead of beginning a pitch. Profit builds because this frames him as an expert running an assessment rather than a salesperson running a presentation. Love builds because Alicia now has a meeting where someone is listening to her problem rather than presenting their solution.

Alicia: "Honestly? Speed. We had three executives relocate last quarter and the agent hand-off timing was inconsistent. One of them went three weeks without an agent contact and escalated to HR."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 78 ▲ 2|LOVE 70 ▲ 2|TAX 14 —

MOVE SPECIFIC DISCLOSURE — HIGH VALUE INTELLIGENCE

Alicia just gave Devon the exact problem she needs solved. Profit ticks up because Devon now has specific, actionable intelligence. This is the moment most BDMs make the critical error: they immediately move to pitch. The scorer holds.

Devon: "Three weeks without contact after a relocation is a retention risk. That's not a real estate problem — that's an HR exposure. I want to come back to you in a week with how we've handled this specific situation for two other corporate accounts and what the response time protocol looks like. Would that be useful?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 88 ▲ 10|LOVE 82 ▲ 12|TAX 10 ▼ 4

MOVE REFRAME + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 01 & 09

Devon did three things. He reframed the problem from real estate to HR exposure — elevating it and himself simultaneously. He declined to pitch immediately, which is the highest-Profit move available in a first Prospect meeting. He created a specific next step with a specific timeline. Profit reaches its peak in this conversation. Love builds 12 points. The scorer marks Devon as having successfully converted a first meeting into a pipeline relationship.

BDM / AGENT

The Pipeline Review

Where the BDM's work either compounds or stalls

Rachel is the BDM. Tyler is her agent. The quarter has been slow. Three referrals from her corporate account did not convert.

◆

Tyler: "I called all three of them. The Harrison account — they're not ready. Said they're looking at Q3."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 58 —|LOVE 62 —|TAX 34 ▲ 8

MOVE MINIMAL REPORT — TAX BUILD

Tyler's report is thin. "Not ready" and "looking at Q3" is not a pipeline analysis — it is a status update with no intelligence attached. Tax builds because Rachel now must decide whether to push for more depth or accept the surface report. This is the BDM/Agent friction point: the agent who does not report back fully is degrading the BDM's ability to manage the Referral Source relationship correctly.

Rachel: "When you spoke to Harrison — what did you learn about what's holding them at Q3? What does their situation actually look like?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▲ 6|LOVE 64 ▲ 2|TAX 26 ▼ 8

MOVE DIAGNOSTIC DEMAND — PROFIT RECOVERY

Rachel ran a precision diagnostic question. Not "did you follow up" but "what did you learn." Profit recovers because she is steering the conversation toward intelligence rather than activity reporting. Tax drops because she is creating the conditions for a more useful analysis.

Tyler: "He mentioned a school district concern. His kids are in middle school and the zoning on the properties I showed him doesn't work for him."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 68 ▲ 4|LOVE 64 —|TAX 22 ▼ 4

MOVE SPECIFIC INTELLIGENCE — PROBLEM IDENTIFIED

Tyler finally surfaced the real information. The school district concern is actionable. Tax drops because the real problem is now visible. The scorer's next question: does Rachel have the intelligence to address this, and does she have properties or referral sources that could solve it?

Rachel: "I have two listings coming in the Eastview district in six weeks. If I get you the specs this week, can you reach back to Harrison with something specific rather than a general follow-up?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 12|LOVE 72 ▲ 8|TAX 14 ▼ 8

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 03 & 09

Rachel converted the problem into a solution in one move. Intelligence Transfer: she had relevant inventory that addressed the specific constraint. Path Forward: she gave Tyler an executable next step with a timeline. Profit builds significantly. The pipeline just moved.

BDM / REFERRAL SOURCE

The Difficult Call

When something went wrong with a referred client

Jordan is a BDM. Sandra is an estate attorney who has referred four clients in the past year. One of those clients had a poor experience — delays in communication, a missed deadline. Sandra is calling.

◆

Sandra: "I need to talk to you about the Nguyen file."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 54 ▼ 10|LOVE 60 —|TAX 52 ▲ 12

MOVE INCOMING DIFFICULT CALL — CRITICAL TAX

Sandra did not explain why she was calling. The opener "I need to talk to you about" in a Referral Source relationship is a high-Tax signal. Profit has dropped before a single substantive word has been said because Jordan's expert position is now under implicit challenge.

pages.title: PART FOUR (cont. 2)
pages.html:
Jordan: "I know. I was going to call you today. The communication on that file was not what it should have been and that is on my team. I want to tell you exactly what happened and what we are changing."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 62 ▲ 8|LOVE 80 ▲ 20|TAX 38 ▼ 14

MOVE OWNERSHIP MOVE — MOVE 05

Jordan ran Move 05 before Sandra could deliver her complaint. This is the move that saves referral relationships. Love builds 20 points — enormous recovery in a single sentence — because Jordan owned it proactively, completely, and without waiting to hear the extent of Sandra's frustration. Tax drops because the defensive position has been abandoned. Profit recovers because Jordan took control of the narrative by admitting rather than explaining.

Sandra: "She called me frustrated. What happened?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 64 ▲ 2|LOVE 82 ▲ 2|TAX 36 ▼ 2

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — SANDRA IS LISTENING

Sandra asked for the facts rather than escalating emotionally. This is a Love signal — the prior relationship has enough balance that she is willing to hear the explanation. The Ownership Move bought Jordan the room to give one.

Jordan: "The agent on this file was managing four closings simultaneously and dropped the communication protocol on day nine. I've put a single-agent maximum of three active files going forward. This will not happen to another client you send us. And I'd like to call Mrs. Nguyen personally if you will allow me to."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 12|LOVE 90 ▲ 8|TAX 24 ▼ 12

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 02 & 09

Jordan named the specific failure, named the specific structural change, and created a specific recovery action for the affected client. Love reaches its highest point in this conversation because Jordan did not defend the failure — they diagnosed it and fixed it in the same breath. The Referral Source relationship survives and, in this case, deepens. This is the BDM Ownership Move at full expression.

BDM / BUILDER

The Institutional Meeting

Where volume relationships are negotiated

Rachel is presenting to the sales director of a regional builder. They have had six transactions together over eighteen months. The builder wants to expand the relationship.

◆

Director: "We're opening two new communities in Q2. We'd like to understand what your team can do at scale."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 68 —|LOVE 68 —|TAX 24 ▲ 6

MOVE SCALE INQUIRY — OPPORTUNITY WITH TAX

The builder is testing capability, not just interest. "At scale" is a Profit question — can Rachel's operation deliver at a volume that justifies institutional commitment? Tax builds because the question creates an obligation to be honest about capacity.

Rachel: "Before I tell you what we can do — I want to make sure I understand what the two communities need specifically. I've done volume builder work where the expectations were misaligned upfront and it created problems mid-stream. I don't want that for either of us."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 78 ▲ 10|LOVE 78 ▲ 10|TAX 16 ▼ 8

MOVE HONEST STRIKE + DIAGNOSTIC — MOVES 02 & 06

Rachel ran the Honest Strike before the pitch. She disclosed a past misalignment experience rather than going directly to capability. Profit builds because she demonstrated that she thinks about operational fit, not just deal volume. Love builds because the director just saw a potential partner who was willing to acknowledge risk before it materialized. Tax drops because Rachel has reframed the conversation as a mutual fit assessment rather than a sales presentation.

Director: "What kind of misalignment?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 80 ▲ 2|LOVE 82 ▲ 4|TAX 14 ▼ 2

MOVE ENGAGEMENT — DIRECTOR IS INVESTING

The director asked a follow-up question about risk. This is the highest-value engagement signal in an institutional meeting — they are doing due diligence rather than processing a pitch. The relationship has moved from vendor evaluation to partner assessment.

Rachel: "Communication frequency during construction delays. Buyers go quiet and then escalate. What I'd want to establish upfront is a shared protocol — your team, my team, agreed touchpoints regardless of news. That prevents the escalations that eat everyone's time."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 88 ▲ 8|LOVE 86 ▲ 4|TAX 10 ▼ 4

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER + PATH FORWARD — MOVES 03 & 09

Rachel solved a problem the director has had before without being asked to solve it. Intelligence Transfer: she brought operational intelligence from prior builder experience. Path Forward: she proposed a specific structural solution. The institutional relationship just moved to a different level.

BDM / COMPETITOR

The Market Conversation

The relationship most BDMs never develop

Devon is at an industry breakfast. He sits next to Keisha, the top BDM at a competing firm. They have seen each other at events for two years but never had a real conversation.

◆

Keisha: "Your team had a strong quarter. The Eastview project — that was smart positioning."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 66 —|LOVE 66 ▲ 4|TAX 24 ▲ 4

MOVE COMPETITOR ACKNOWLEDGMENT — MARKET INTELLIGENCE SIGNAL

Keisha knows Devon's work. She has been watching. The acknowledgment is not small talk — it is a signal that she respects his operation enough to track it. Love ticks up because genuine acknowledgment from a peer is meaningful. Tax ticks up because Devon now has to decide how open to be with a competitor.

Devon: "Your corporate relocation volume — I noticed you picked up two accounts I was also talking to. You got there first. What are you doing differently on the corporate side?"

THE SCORE

PROFIT 72 ▲ 6|LOVE 74 ▲ 8|TAX 18 ▼ 6

MOVE HONEST INQUIRY — PROFIT AND LOVE BUILD

Devon asked a direct, honest question of a competitor. He acknowledged she outperformed him on specific business and asked how. This is a high-Profit, high-Love move because it demonstrates both confidence and genuine curiosity. Most BDMs would deflect from this conversation. Devon went directly into it.

Keisha: "Response time on the initial intake. Corporate coordinators have told us it's the number one differentiator. We built a 90-minute response protocol."

THE SCORE

PROFIT 76 ▲ 4|LOVE 80 ▲ 6|TAX 14 ▼ 4

MOVE INTELLIGENCE TRANSFER FROM COMPETITOR — RARE AND VALUABLE

Keisha just gave Devon her operational intelligence. Why? Because Devon's honest acknowledgment built enough Love in this conversation for her to treat him as a peer rather than a threat. The competitor conversation that begins with honesty and genuine curiosity produces intelligence that the transactional competitor relationship never generates.

pages.title: PART FIVE
pages.html:
PART FIVE

The Drills

Score the BDM move. Train the long-game eye.

BDM drills are scored differently from other editions. The score movement in a BDM conversation is often smaller per line — the big movements happen over multiple interactions. The skill being trained here is pattern recognition: which direction is this relationship moving, and why.

DRILL 01

"I'll have something for you soon."

Score this follow-up commitment. What is actually happening to the score?

ANSWER P −4 · L −2 · T +10

Tax +10. This is the most consistently Tax-building phrase in BDM conversations. "Soon" is not a date. "Something" is not a deliverable. The contact has been given an implied promise with no mechanism for accountability. The BDM who says this is not managing their pipeline — they are managing their discomfort about not yet having something to deliver. Replace it every time with Move 09: a specific deliverable and a specific date.

DRILL 02

"I saw this article and thought of you."

Score this outreach move. Is it a Profit move, Love move, or Tax move?

ANSWER P +4 · L +8 · T −4

Love +8, Profit +4. This is Intelligence Transfer in its simplest form — and it is one of the highest-ROI moves in BDM outreach. A contact who receives relevant, specific content from a BDM who thought of them specifically registers both the value of the content and the quality of the attention. Profit builds because the BDM has demonstrated they know what is relevant to this contact's world. Tax drops because the outreach had no ask attached.

DRILL 03

"Let me know if you ever need anything."

Score this closing line at the end of a lunch meeting.

ANSWER P −6 · L −4 · T +8

Tax +8. "Let me know if you ever need anything" is the BDM equivalent of a dead end. It creates a vague standing offer that the contact will almost never activate because it requires them to do the work of identifying the need and initiating the ask. Love drops because the closing lacked intention. Profit drops because the BDM ended the meeting without establishing a clear next value exchange. Replace with Move 09 every time: a specific next step with a specific purpose.

DRILL 04

"I want to introduce you to someone who could be useful to your business."

Score this outreach. What is the Profit position of the BDM running this move?

ANSWER P +12 · L +10 · T −6

BDM Profit +12, Love +10. This is the Intelligence Transfer at relationship scale. The BDM who introduces two valuable people to each other creates Profit capital with both of them simultaneously. Love builds with both contacts. Tax drops because the move has no visible agenda — the BDM is giving away value with no explicit return requested. The BDM who runs this consistently across their portfolio becomes the person nobody can afford to lose from their network.

DRILL 05

"We've been working together for a while now — I wanted to ask if there are other parts of your business I could be more useful to."

Score this mature relationship move.

ANSWER P +8 · L +12 · T −8

Love +12, Profit +8. This is Move 06 — Pressure Reveal — applied to a positive context. The BDM is surfacing an opportunity for expanded partnership by acknowledging the existing relationship as the foundation. Love builds because the contact hears genuine investment in the relationship rather than a pitch. Profit builds because the BDM has positioned themselves as a strategic partner rather than a service provider. Tax drops because the conversation is explicitly about giving more, not asking for more.

DRILL 06

"I heard you might be working with one of our competitors."

Score this competitive intelligence probe.

ANSWER P −8 · L −12 · T +16

Tax +16. This is one of the most dangerous moves in BDM work. If the information is accurate, the contact now knows their business is being tracked by competitors — which builds immediate distrust. If inaccurate, the BDM has introduced a false assumption and damaged credibility. Love drops sharply because the contact feels surveilled rather than valued. The scorer marks this as a move that should almost never be run. If competitive intelligence suggests a contact is shifting, the correct move is Move 03 — bring them something of value and let the relationship speak for itself.

DRILL 07

"I don't have an answer to that right now but I will find out and call you by Thursday."

Score this response to a difficult question from a referral source.

ANSWER P +4 · L +16 · T −8

Love +16. This is the Honest Strike in its simplest professional form. The BDM does not know the answer. They said so. They committed to a specific answer with a specific deadline. Love builds enormously because Referral Sources have been lied to by vendors more times than they can count — the BDM who admits "I don't know" and commits to finding out becomes the rarest kind of professional in their network: the kind they can actually trust.

DRILL 08

"We had a situation I need to tell you about before you hear about it from someone else."

Score this proactive disclosure to a partner.

ANSWER P +6 · L +18 · T 0

Love +18. The highest Love-building move in BDM work. Proactive disclosure of a problem — before the partner could have heard about it independently — is the Honest Strike at its most complete. Profit builds because the BDM has demonstrated they manage their relationships rather than their reputation. Tax stays flat because disclosure does not reduce the obligation created by the problem — but it prevents the additional Tax of being caught managing the information rather than the situation.

pages.title: PART SIX
pages.html:
PART SIX

The Field Guide

Every BDM situation. What to watch. What it means. Your move.

Building the Relationship

THE FIRST MEETING WITH A NEW PROSPECT

WATCH The prospect talks more than 60% of the meeting.

MEANS The diagnostic questions are working. The prospect has converted from a receiving posture to a disclosing posture.

YOUR MOVE Do not redirect to your pitch. Keep asking. The more they disclose in the first meeting, the more precisely you can run Move 03 in the follow-up. The first meeting's score is measured entirely in intelligence gained.

THE PROSPECT ASKS WHAT YOU DO BEFORE YOU ASK YOUR FIRST QUESTION

WATCH The prospect opened with "so tell me about your company."

MEANS They have come prepared to evaluate a pitch, not engage in a discovery conversation. They are in receiving mode.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 04 — Evidence Mirror: "I will, but I want to make sure what I tell you is actually relevant to your situation. Can I ask you one question first?" This resets the frame from pitch meeting to diagnostic conversation. Profit is won or lost in the first three exchanges.

A CONTACT GOES QUIET AFTER A PERIOD OF REGULAR ENGAGEMENT

WATCH Response times have lengthened. Meetings are being pushed. The energy has changed.

MEANS The Love account is draining or the Tax has built to a level they are not ready to articulate.

YOUR MOVE Do not follow up with another ask. Run Move 03 — Intelligence Transfer. Send something valuable with no ask attached. If they respond, the relationship is recoverable. If they do not, the Tax has exceeded the Love and the correct move is to give the relationship space.

Managing the Partnership

A PARTNER BRINGS YOU THEIR BEST CLIENT

WATCH The introduction is detailed, warm, and includes specific context about the client's needs.

MEANS The partner's Love account with you is at its highest point. They are extending their reputation on your behalf.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 02 — Honest Strike if there is any complexity in the client's situation: "I want to make sure I understand exactly what they need so I can tell you honestly if we are the right fit." This protects the partner's relationship with their client if the situation is complex.

A REFERRED CLIENT TRANSACTION HAS A PROBLEM

WATCH Something has gone wrong on a file from a valued referral source.

MEANS The Tax is building in the referral relationship even if the referral source does not know the details yet.

YOUR MOVE Call the referral source before they hear from the client. Run Move 05 — Ownership Move. Do not wait to resolve the problem first. Own it, state what is being done, and commit to a specific update timeline. The referral source who learns about a problem from the client rather than from you does not send another referral.

A PARTNER ASKS FOR A REFERRAL YOU ARE NOT CONFIDENT MAKING

WATCH The partner has asked you to send clients to someone you do not fully know.

MEANS Sending a client to an unvetted partner is high Tax against your relationship with that client.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 02 — Honest Strike: "I want to know your work better before I send anyone to you. Let me spend some time understanding how you operate and then I'll be able to introduce you with confidence." This protects your clients and signals to the partner that your referrals mean something.

Growing the Pipeline

AN INSTITUTIONAL CONTACT ASKS ABOUT EXPANDING THE RELATIONSHIP

WATCH The builder or corporate account is signaling interest in more volume.

MEANS This is a Profit and Tax conversation simultaneously. More volume means more Love potential and more operational exposure.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 06 — Pressure Reveal: identify the specific risk in scaling before accepting the opportunity. "I want to make sure we grow this correctly. The places I've seen volume partnerships fail are X and Y — let's address those upfront." This builds more institutional trust than agreeing immediately.

A COMPETITOR REACHES OUT FOR A POTENTIAL COLLABORATION

WATCH A competitor is approaching you about a referral arrangement or overflow partnership.

MEANS This is the highest-Profit potential and highest-Tax risk conversation in BDM work. Competitor partnerships that are not well-defined create obligations that are difficult to enforce.

YOUR MOVE Run Move 04 — Evidence Mirror before committing: "Let me understand how you've handled this type of arrangement before." Get specific data on prior collaborations before agreeing to the structure. Intelligence first.

THE QUARTERLY REVIEW SHOWS PIPELINE VOLUME HAS DROPPED

WATCH Fewer referrals are coming in from relationships that were previously active.

MEANS Scores have drained in relationships that appeared to be healthy. The activity reports showed engagement but the Love accounts were coasting.

YOUR MOVE Audit the three most important relationships in your portfolio. When did you last run Move 03 on each of them — give them something of genuine value with no ask attached? Pipeline volume follows Love account balance, usually on a sixty to ninety day lag.

The pipeline is not a funnel.

It is a ledger.

Every contact in your network has an account balance you are managing whether you know it or not. Profit, Love, and Tax — building, draining, compounding in every conversation you have and every conversation you do not have. The BDM who scores those accounts correctly does not have a pipeline problem. They have a timing problem at worst — they know which relationships are ready, which ones need investment, and which ones are signaling that the balance has shifted.

The scorer does not wait for the referral to see how the relationship is doing. The scorer reads the conversation that happened two months ago and knows what the referral volume will look like next quarter.

That is the BDM at full expression. Not a relationship manager. Not a pipeline generator. A scorer.

Profit. Love. Tax.

Every relationship. Long game.

About the Author

Craig Jones is the founder of the PLT Framework and the architect of the PLT Doctrine Series. He writes under the name Little Bunny. The PLT Framework was built from direct observation of how high-stakes conversations actually work — what gets exchanged, what gets built, and what quietly drains in the conversations that shape careers and pipelines. The Scorer: BDM is the application of that doctrine to the profession built entirely on relationships.
